beats.narration_text: Hello, I'm Vineet S.. A prompt is the closest thing a product manager has to a steering wheel for an A I product. A few sentences can change its tone, its accuracy and its safety. Let's look at how prompts shape behavior, and how to manage them like product.

The user prompt carries the request

beats.narration_text: Prompting is writing a clear spec, then testing it on real cases. There are no magic words. There is a specification, an example, a test, and a revision, which is exactly how a product manager already works.

props.text:

that make it work.

props.replacementWords: writing a clear spec, then testing it on real cases

beats.narration_text: Here are the five pieces. The system prompt. The user prompt. Few-shot examples. Prompt testing. And prompt iteration. The first three shape behavior. The last two make sure the behavior is good, and stays good.

The system prompt is written by the product team. It sets the role, the rules, the tone and the limits. Users usually never see it, but they feel it in every answer. The user prompt is what the person types. The model reads both together.

layers.sub: Written by you: role, rules, tone, limits

layers.title: User prompt
layers.sub: Written by the user: the actual request

beats.narration_text: Watch how they combine. The system prompt, the rules and tone, and the user's message all flow into one answer. For example, a support assistant told to be friendly, concise and to cite the policy will answer the same question very differently from one told to be formal and detailed. Every line in a system prompt is a product decision.

props.arcCaption: For example: friendly, concise, cites policy

beats.narration_text: Few-shot prompting means including a few examples of good input and output in the prompt. With zero examples, the model relies on your instructions alone. Examples show format, tone and edge cases far better than description does. But choose them carefully, because the model copies their patterns, including accidental ones.

layers.title: Few-shot
layers.sub: Add a few input and output examples

layers.title: Why it works
layers.sub: Examples show format, tone and edge cases

beats.narration_text: Prompts need tests, just like code. Run a fixed set of cases every time you change a prompt. Include edge cases and adversarial inputs, like users trying to override the rules. Keep inputs the same across runs, score outputs with a rubric, and compare versions side by side. And because outputs can vary, run important cases more than once.

props.caption: A prompt change is a release

beats.narration_text: Then iterate, deliberately. Change one thing at a time, so you know what caused the effect. Run the test set and compare to the last version. Keep what wins, and save every version with notes. And keep watching in production, because real users will find failures your tests did not.

layers.title: Change one thing
layers.sub: So you know what caused the effect

beats.narration_text: So, prompt engineering. The system prompt sets behavior. Examples teach format. Tests prove it works. And every change is an experiment you can compare.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. I am a product manager building an AI assistant that does this: [describe it]. Write a first system prompt with a role, rules, tone and limits. Add three few-shot examples, including one tricky case. Then give me ten test inputs, five normal and five adversarial, and a rubric to score the answers. Finally, tell me which line of the system prompt is most likely to be ignored. The last sentence is the sharp one. Some instructions are followed less reliably than others, so find the line Claude thinks is weakest, and write a test for it first. Pause here and run it on your own product.
